overview: Benone Strand is part of a seven-mile run of golden sand on the north coast of County Londonderry, overlooked by the cliffs and mountain of Binevenagh with views across to Donegal. The council describes the sand as clean and firm, with no rocks, shingle or seaweed — a rare thing on an Atlantic coast, and a big reason it works so well for learning.

It sits within the Binevenagh Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and its dunes are protected as part of the Magilligan Special Area of Conservation. Boardwalks and a waymarked trail cross the dunes from the entrance, and the area is known for its botany, insects and shells. In 2017 it became Northern Ireland's first fully inclusive beach, through the council's work with the Mae Murray Foundation.

Parking is free at the entrance and on the beach itself, and the Ark building at the entrance houses toilets and a coffee dock. The council sets out zones for swimming, jet skis, dogs and other activities, so look at the signs before you set up. With so much sand you can always find space, but facilities thin out quickly as you walk away from the entrance.
notFor: Anyone wanting cliffs and coves — it is an open strand

text: Benone is an open sandy beach break with lefts and rights spread along the strand. Forecast sites rate the strand best on a north-westerly swell with offshore winds from the south-east. Firm sand and the lack of rocks make it forgiving for learners, but it is still an exposed Atlantic beach and is more demanding as the swell builds.
Banks move after storms, and rips can form between them. Use the zoned areas and stay between the flags when lifeguards are on duty. Further east towards Downhill the beach is a little more exposed.

Benone is a long, shifty beach break: the sandbanks move with the tides and the swell, so the working peak can be anywhere along the strand, and you often have to walk to find it. It likes a north-westerly to northerly swell and works best on smaller days, roughly knee-high to head-high, with a south-south-easterly wind blowing offshore. It works at all tides, with a rising tide generally better.

It's usually quiet, and the waves are generally smaller and gentler than elsewhere on the coast, which suits beginners and intermediates on a fish, funboard or longboard. Rips and currents get stronger as the surf gets bigger, and after heavy rain there can be farm runoff in the water. Autumn, winter and spring are the seasons, with winter the strongest. A surf school operates on the beach.

cards.label: Level
cards.title: Beginners to intermediates
cards.text: Firm, rock-free sand makes it one of the best learner beaches in the region.

cards.label: Conditions
cards.title: NW swell, south-east wind
cards.text: Best small, knee to head high; the working peak moves with the banks.

cards.label: Season
cards.title: Autumn to spring
cards.text: Winter is strongest; summer is often flat.

cards.label: Hazards
cards.title: Rips and vehicles
cards.text: Rips that strengthen with size, shifting banks and cars on the sand.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Free
practical.text: At the beach entrance and on the beach, with accessible parking.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: The Ark
practical.text: Accessible toilets and a coffee dock at the entrance. Beach access equipment can be booked through the Mae Murray Foundation.

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: Seasonal RNLI patrol
practical.text: The council lists a seasonal RNLI patrol, 10am–6pm daily in July and August. Check the RNLI site for this year's dates.

practical.label: Dogs
practical.title: Summer restrictions
practical.text: Dogs are allowed, with restrictions from 1 June to 15 September (the Blue Flag season). Use the dog zone.

practical.label: Nature
practical.title: Protected dunes
practical.text: Part of the Binevenagh AONB and Magilligan Special Area of Conservation — keep to the boardwalks.

faqs.q: Is Benone good for learning to surf?
faqs.a: Yes. The sand is firm and rock-free, there are lifeguards in July and August, and the activity zones keep surfers apart from other users.
Yes, at the entrance and on the beach.
It was Northern Ireland's first fully inclusive beach, with accessible parking, toilets and bookable beach equipment.
Yes, with restrictions from 1 June to 15 September.
